Across the two tables, several key findings emerge. First, **GoogLeNet with transfer learning** is the strongest overall configuration, reaching a mean F1 of 0.9934 on color images with an 80/20 train/test split, while **AlexNet trained from scratch on grayscale images with minimal training data (20/80 split)** performs worst (F1 = 0.8524). Second, three factors systematically improve detection performance: **using transfer learning over training from scratch, using color images over grayscale or segmented inputs, and increasing the proportion of training data**, with all three effects consistent across architectures and splits. Third, **precision, recall, and accuracy closely track mean F1 scores** in every experimental configuration, indicating robust and balanced performance rather than trade-offs among metrics. Finally, the models were trained using a **standard SGD setup** (learning rate 0.005, step-based decay of ×10, momentum 0.9), underscoring that these strong results are achievable with well-established hyperparameters rather than exotic tuning—reinforcing the practical viability of deep CNNs (especially transfer-learned GoogLeNet) for accurate image-based plant disease detection even with limited training data.
